:::{#def-continuous-several}
#### Continuity in several variables

A function $f$ from $\reals^p$ to $\reals^q$ is **continuous at** $\vx$
if for every $\tolout > 0$ there is a $\tolin > 0$ such that
$\norm{f(\vy) - f(\vx)} < \tolout$ whenever $\norm{\vy - \vx} < \tolin$.
It is **continuous on** a set if it is continuous at every point of the set.
For $q = 1$, $\norm{f(\vy) - f(\vx)} = \abs{f(\vy) - f(\vx)}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-continuous-several}
#### A continuous function, and a discontinuous one

- $f(\vx) = x_1 + x_2$ is continuous at every $\vx$.
  Each $\abs{y_i - x_i} \le \norm{\vy - \vx}$, since the squared length is a sum of nonnegative squares, so

  $$
  \ba
  \abs{f(\vy) - f(\vx)}
  &= \abs{(y_1 - x_1) + (y_2 - x_2)}
  && \text{(subtract)}
  \\
  &\le \abs{y_1 - x_1} + \abs{y_2 - x_2}
  && \text{(triangle inequality for numbers)}
  \\
  &\le 2\,\norm{\vy - \vx},
  && \text{(each term is at most } \norm{\vy - \vx} \text{)}
  \ea
  $$

  which is less than $\tolout$ whenever $\norm{\vy - \vx} < \tolin = \tolout / 2$.
- $f(\vx) = 1$ if $x_1 > 0$ and $f(\vx) = 0$ otherwise is not continuous at $\vzero$:
  for $\tolout = \tfrac{1}{2}$ and any $\tolin > 0$, the point $\vy = \tp{(\tolin / 2, 0)}$
  has $\norm{\vy - \vzero} = \tolin / 2 < \tolin$ but $\abs{f(\vy) - f(\vzero)} = 1 > \tfrac{1}{2}$.

:::
